title: Correlation between microstructure and shape memory properties in an Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn dual phase steel developed by intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing
abstract: Research was conducted to investigate the shape memory properties related to the microstructure in an Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) dual phase steel developed by intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing. Electron back scattering diffraction (EBSD) analysis and high resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) images revealed that the microstructure of the initial steel in the solution-annealed condition was a typical lath α′-martensite with a high density of dislocations. During the intercritical annealing treatment of the solution-annealed steel at 590 °C in the ferritic-austenitic (α+γ) two-phase region for various annealing times, a part of α′-martensite transformed to the reversed γ-austenite with a difusionless shear nature, resulting in the development of a dual-phase (α′+γ) steel. Also, subsequent ageing treatment of the intercritically annealed steel at 480 °C for 3.6 ks led to formation of the nanoscale θ-NiMn precipitates in the dual-phase microstructure. The experimental results indicated a maximum shape recovery of ∼55% at 1% pre-strain for the intercritically annealed steel for 1.8 ks, followed by subsequent ageing. The presence of austenite phase reinforced by precipitates in the dual-phase steel was the main reason for appearance the shape recovery. In addition, the existence of isolated stacking faults in the reversed austenite region after straining confirmed that the occurrence of the austenite to ε-martensite transformation (γ→ε) under loading and the reverse transformation (ε→γ) upon heating are the main causes of the shape memory effect in the studied steel.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Among the different shape memory alloys (SMAs), Fe-based SMAs are more suitable for large-scale industrial applications due to their low alloying cost and good workability [ 1–3 ]. These materials can be used as damping and clamping devices, pipe joints and rail couplings in mechanical engineering and also for the reinforcement of concrete and girders by internally activated pre-stressing in civil engineering [ 4–6 ]. The shape memory effect (SME) in these SMAs is related to strain-induced austenite to martensite transformation under loading and its reverse transformation upon heating [ 7 , 8 ]. Fe-based SMAs have also a unique behavior of pseudoelasticity (PE). In this behavior, a certain fraction of non-linear strain can be recovered upon unloading [ 9 ]. It was reported that the polycrystalline Fe-based SMAs have a low recovery strain in the solution-annealed condition [ 10 , 11 ]. Therefore, in the three past decades, considerable efforts were conducted to improve the SME and PE behavior in Fe-based SMAs such as composition design [ 12–15 ], thermo-mechanical treatments [ 16 , 17 ], training [ 18–20 ], and precipitation hardening [ 21–25 ]. Improvements in the achieved SME and PE were associated with increase in the yield strength of the austenite phase and reduction in the critical stress required for the martensitic transformation in all of these attempts.

Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) low carbon steel has a fully lath α′-martensite microstructure in the solution-annealed condition [ 26 , 27 ]. It is prone to age hardening due to the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates [ 26–29 ]. To observe the behavior of SME and PE in this alloy, the austenite (γ) phase must be introduced into the martensite matrix so that a dual phase (α′+γ) steel is developed. Intercritical annealing in dual phase (ferrite + austenite) region is one of the main methods for stabilizing the austenite phase at room temperature [ 30 , 31 ]. During this treatment, the austenite phase can be formed in the martensite matrix through the occurrence of the reverse transformation of martensite to the austenite [ 32–36 ]. It is reported that there are two main mechanisms for austenite formation under the reverse transformation consisting of diffusional and diffusionless shear mechanisms. Heating rate, annealing temperature and annealing time are the main factors that determine the mechanism of the reverse transformation. Austenite phase with equiaxed morphology and low dislocation density has a diffusional nature, while lath-shaped reversed austenite with a high density of dislocation indicates the occurrence of diffusionless transformation [ 34–36 ]. Ageing treatment of the Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn steel increases the hardness and strength of the alloy due to the formation of the nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates in the microstructure [ 37 , 38 ]. Therefore, precipitates formation in the microstructure of the intercritacally annealed Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn steel after a subsequent ageing treatment can improve the SME and PE behavior in this alloy.

Detailed examinations show that although there are some studies on the PE behavior of the Fe–Ni–Mn steels [ 38–41 ], the SME of the intercritically annealed Fe–Ni–Mn low carbon steels has not been evaluated to date. Thus, the present research aims, for the first time, to systematically investigate the influence of intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments on the microstructure and shape memory properties of an Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn martensitic steel.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs:
An ingot of Fe–9Ni-6.5Mn (at.%) steel was casted three times in a vacuum arc re-melting furnace at 10 −3  mbar using high purity iron, electrolytic manganese, and pure nickel shots. The chemical composition of the alloy in wt.% is given in  Table 1 
                      . The prepared ingot was forged by 50% reduction at 1200 °C to break the dendritic cast structure and then homogenized at 1150 °C for 86.4 ks in an atmospherically controlled tube furnace. Then, solution annealing was carried out at 950 °C for 3.6 ks followed by water quenching to room temperature. Four specimens were cut from the solution-annealed (SA) ingot for subsequent heat treatments.

Adamel-DT1000 dilatometer was used to measure the phase transformation temperatures. The tested sample was cut from the SA alloy and machined to cylindrical specimen with a length and diameter of 10 and 2.4 mm, respectively. The specimen was heated to 700 °C at a linear rate of 0.05 °C/s to simulate the slow heating process of the alloy, and then cooled to room temperature at a rate of 20 °C/s.

To induce the austenite phase into the martensite matrix, the SA specimens were subjected to intercritical annealing at 590 °C in the ferritic-austenitic (α+γ) two phase region for 0.9, 1.8, 3.6, and 7.2 ks. Subsequently, the intercritically annealed (IA) specimens were aged at 480 C for 3.6 ks.

Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) system operated at 15 kV with a step size of 0.2 μm was used to observe the microstructures. For this purpose, the surface of specimens mechanically polished and then electro-etched in a solution with a composition of 90% CH 3 COOH and 10% HClO 4 . To further observe microstructures, a high resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) model PHILIPS CM200-FEG operating at 200 kV was used. Disk-shaped HRTEM specimens were electro-polished using the double-jet technique in an electrolyte solution composed of CrO 3 , CH 3 COOH and H 2 O at room temperature. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns obtained from the different specimens were indexed according to the method explained by Cullity and Stock [ 42 ].
Vickers microhardness (Hv) was measured in five different points of each specimen using a hardness machine with an applied load of 100 gf.

SME was measured using tensile test and recovery annealing. Sheet-type tensile test samples were cut from the subsequently aged-IA specimens for various annealing times with thickness of 1 mm, width of 5.5 mm, and gage length of 14 mm. Tensile test was performed on prepared specimens at different pre-strains (1, 2, 4, 6 and 8%). For each pre-strain, three tensile test samples were examined. After that, shape recovery (SR) of the deformed specimens was achieved by annealing at 700 °C (above A f  temperature) for 1.2 ks.  Fig. 1

sections.heading: Measurement of phase transformation temperatures
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          shows the dilatation curve as a function of temperature for the SA specimen under heating up to 700 °C and then cooling to room temperature. It is clear that the reverse transformation of martensite to austenite under heating is accompanied by contraction due to the crystal structure adjustment from bcc to fcc. The drastic changes observed in the dilatation curves and marked as the austenite start (A s ) and finish (A f ) temperatures are discussed bellow.

A smooth deviation from the linear curve preceding the A s  temperature under heating is shown in  Fig. 3 . One can propose that such a kind of deviation is correlated with the θ-NiMn precipitates formation which has been reported in previous researches [ 26–29 ]. The precipitation start (P s ) and finish (P f ) temperatures are also marked on the figure which are ∼415 and ∼525 °C, respectively. According to the figure, it is proposed that the A s  and A f  temperatures are close to 570 and 640 °C, respectively. By cooling the SA specimen after being heated up to 700 °C, the forward transformation of austenite to martensite starts and finishes at temperatures about 225 °C and 110 °C, respectively. The mentioned temperatures are respectively martensite start (M s ) and finish (M f ) temperatures.

sections.heading: Microstructure of the SA specimen
paragraphs:
Fig. 4 
                            (a) shows a bright field HRTEM image of the SA specimen demonstrating the typical lath α′-martensite with a high density of dislocations. It is apparent that the average lath thickness of martensite is ∼150 nm. The grain boundary and phase map of the SA specimen obtained from EBSD analysis is also displayed in  Fig. 4 (b), where the red and black lines correspond to the low angle grain boundary (LAGBs: 2° ≤ θ < 15°) and high angle grain boundary (HAGBs: θ ≥ 15°), respectively. The LAGBs are indicative of the presence of dislocations in the microstructure [ 43 , 44 ]. Also, the pink and yellow colors exhibit the α′-martensite and γ-austenite phases, respectively. According to the EBSD image, the SA specimen's microstructure contains of fully lath α′-martensite with a high density of dislocations.

sections.heading: Microstructure of the IA specimens before and after subsequent ageing
paragraphs:
The phase maps of the IA specimens at 590 °C for various annealing times are illustrated in  Fig. 5 
                            . The pink color exhibits α′-martensite phase and the yellow color denotes γ-austenite phase. It is obvious that under intercritical annealing treatment, the austenite phase uniformly introduces at the martensite matrix and a two-phase microstructure consisting of α′-martensite and γ-austenite (α′+γ) is developed. The nucleation of the reversed austenite grains occurs at the packet and block boundaries as well as at the grain boundaries of the martensite matrix [ 45 , 46 ]. In addition, the grains of austenite have a high density of LAGBs due to the presence of dislocations in this phase. This indicates that the reversed austenite inherits the dislocation structure from the lath α′-martensite. According to  Fig. 5 (a)–5(d), the amount of retained austenite increases with increasing annealing time up to 3.6 ks and then decreases at a later stage of reversion.

Fig. 6 
                             represents the calculated volume fractions of retained austenite at room temperature for the IA specimens at 590 °C for various annealing times. The results were obtained from the EBSD data. It is evident that the amount of retained austenite in the IA specimen for 0.9 ks is ∼17%, which increases by increasing annealing time to a maximum value of ∼45% at 3.6 ks, and then declines at a later stage of reversion to ∼35% for the IA specimen for 7.2 ks.

Chemical composition analysis of the retained austenite at room temperature for the IA specimens at 590 °C for various annealing times is shown in  Fig. 7 
                            . The results were obtained by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). It is clear that the concentrations of Ni and Mn elements are nearly constant and the same with the nominal composition of the SA specimen irrespective of the annealing time.

Bright field HRTEM images with corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns of the IA specimens at 590 °C for 1.8 ks before and after subsequent ageing treatment at 480 °C for 3.6 ks are shown in  Fig. 8 
                            . The bright field HRTEM image in  Fig. 8 (a) represents that the microstructure of the IA specimen consists of the lath-shaped austenite (γ) with a high density of dislocations in the α′-martensite matrix. As indicated in  Fig. 8 (b), the SAED patterns taken at the martensite and austenite areas confirm the formation of lath-shaped austenite in the martensite matrix.  Fig. 8 (c) and (d) respectively show the bright field HRTEM image and the corresponding SAED pattern of the IA specimen for 1.8 ks followed by subsequent ageing. The microstructure in  Fig. 8 (c) clearly shows the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates in the aged-IA specimen. As shown in  Fig. 8 (d), the precipitate formation occurs only in the α′-martensite region.

sections.heading: Microhardness measurments
paragraphs:
Fig. 9 
                          represents Vickers microhardness measurements of the IA specimens for various annealing times before and after subsequent ageing. For the IA specimen for 0.9 ks, the microhardness value is ∼350 Hv which decreases by increasing the annealing time up to a minimum value of ∼280 Hv at 3.6 ks. After that, by more increase in the annealing time, the microhardness increases so that its value reaches ∼295 Hv for the IA specimen for 7.2 ks. For the subsequently aged specimens, the microhardness values are higher than that of the non-aged ones for all of the annealing times. This higher microhardness is related to formation of the θ-NiMn precipitates with a hard nature in the microstructure. The trend of change in microhardness as a function of annealing time is similar for the aged IA specimens as for the un-aged specimens. The value of microhardness for the aged-IA specimen for 0.9 ks is ∼495 Hv, which decreases to ∼360 Hv for the aged-IA specimen for 3.6 ks. By more increasing the annealing time, the microhardness value increases again and ultimately reaches ∼410 Hv for the aged-IA specimen for 7.2 ks.

sections.heading: Shape recovery
paragraphs:
The shape recovery as a function of pre-strain for the aged-IA specimens for various annealing times is plotted in  Fig. 10 
                         (a). A common trend for all specimens is that the shape recovery decreases continuously by increasing pre-strain. It is apparent that the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks has the highest shape recovery for the entire pre-strain range.  Fig. 10 (b) illustrates the effect of annealing time on the maximum shape recovery obtained for the aged-IA specimens. It can be seen that the maximum value of the shape recovery for the aged-IA specimen for 0.9 ks is ∼32% which increases to ∼55% with an increase in annealing time to 1.8 ks. Thereafter, with a further increase in annealing time to 3.6 ks, the maximum shape recovery drops to ∼40%. Finally, this value increases again to ∼48% for the aged-IA specimen for 7.2 ks.

Fig. 11 
                          exhibits the recovery strain as a function of pre-strain for the aged-IA specimens for various annealing times. It is evident that the recovery strain increases sharply for all specimens with an increase in pre-strain from 1% to 2%, and thereafter this increase continues with a lower slope. The highest recovery strain with a value of ∼1.92% is obtained for the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks at a pre-strain of 8%.

Bright field HRTEM image of the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks after applying 1% pre-strain alongside with the SAED pattern are shown in  Fig. 12 
                         . According to  Fig. 12 (a), it is well clear the existence of isolated stacking faults in the reversed austenite region with a high density of scattered dislocations which shown by white circle. In addition, the SAED pattern and the key diagram in  Fig. 12 (b) illustrate the epsilon (ε) martensite pattern. The observation of stacking faults in  Fig. 12  and shape recovery in  Fig. 10  confirm that strain-induced austenite to ε-martensite transformation (γ→ε) upon straining and its reversion (ε→γ) upon heating are the main causes of shape recovery which will be discussed in more detail in section  4 .

sections.heading: Microstructure and phase evolution
paragraphs: According to  Fig. 4 , it is clear that the microstructure of the SA specimen contains a fully lath martensite phase with a high density of dislocations. The lath thickness in the microstructure is ∼150 nm. In general, the lath martensitic microstructure in low carbon martensitic steels consists of martensite lath, block and packet [ 47 ]. Lath is a single crystal of martensite with a high density of dislocations. The block is known as a variant of martensite, containing the laths with the same crystallographic orientation. Also, the packet includes of blocks having the same plane of the parent austenite [ 47–49 ]. Performing the intercritical annealing treatment on the SA specimen leads to introduction of the austenite phase into the lath martensite matrix ( Fig. 5 ). During this heat treatment, the reverse transformation of martensite to austenite takes place, resulting in a dual phase steel consisting of the reversed γ-austenite and α′-martensite. In addition, there is a high density of dislocations in the austenite phase, indicating that the dislocations structure is inherited from the lath martensite to the reversed austenite. The inheritance of dislocation structure in the reversed austenite phase suggests that the reverse transformation from martensite to austenite likely occurs through a diffusionless shear mechanism. Furthermore, according to  Fig. 7 , the constant concentration of Ni and Mn elements in the austenite region in the IA specimens for different annealing times emphasizes that the austenite phase has a diffusionless shear nature.

Based on the EBSD images in  Fig. 5  and the bar graphs in  Fig. 6 , it is revealed that the volume fraction of retained austenite at room temperature increases significantly with increasing annealing time, up to a maximum value of ∼45% at 3.6 ks, and then declines at the further time of reversion. It is important to note that the austenite formed by diffusionless shear mechanism contains a high density of dislocations. By increasing the annealing time, the shear-formed austenite is recovered so that its grains are divided into sub-grains or dislocation cells. Then, the sub-grains transform to fine re-crystallized grains by lattice rotation or merging the cell boundaries [ 50–52 ]. By refining the austenite grains size, the M s  temperature declines, and the re-transformation of the reversed austenite to the fresh martensite is partially suppressed [ 53 ]. Therefore, the amount of retained austenite at room temperature increases with increasing annealing time up to 3.6 ks. After that, by more increasing the annealing time, the austenite grains size increase due to in situ re-crystalization and sub-grain growth, respectively, leading to increase in the M s  temperature and decline the amount of retained austenite.

From the HRTEM image of the IA specimen for 1.8 ks in  Fig. 8 (a), it is obvious that the reversed austenite has the lath-shaped morphology accompanied by a large density of dislocations. These observations are consistent with the EBSD results and confirm that the reversed austenite has a diffusionless shear nature. It was reported that the lath-shaped morphology with a high density of dislocations was a characteristic of shear-formed austenite [ 34–36 ]. After subsequent ageing, as shown in  Fig. 8 (c), the nano-sized θ-NiMn particles precipitate in the microstructure of the aged-IA specimen. It is important to note that the precipitation occurs only in the martensite phase and there is no trace of θ-NiMn particles in the austenite region. Super-saturated nature of the martensitic matrix from the chemical composition aspect is the main reason for the nucleation of the precipitates in this region [ 28 , 29 , 37 ].

sections.heading: Microhardness evaluation
paragraphs: Based on the microhardness measurements of the IA specimens in  Fig. 9  and considering the EBSD images and bar graphs in  Figs. 5 and 6 , respectively, it appears that by increasing the annealing time up to 3.6 ks, the microhardness value decreases due to the increase in the volume fraction of retained austenite with a soft character. After that, by increasing the annealing time to 7.2 ks, the microhardness value increases again because of decrement in the amount of the retained austenite. For the aged-IA specimens, the microhardness values are higher than for the non-aged samples at all annealing times. This is related to the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates with a hard and brittle nature in the microstructure. Since the precipitates nucleate only in the martensite phase and no traces of them are found in the austenite region, the trend of microhardness changes in the aged-IA specimens is the same as in the non-aged specimens. In this case, by increasing the annealing time up to 3.6 ks, the volume fraction of precipitates decreases due to increase of the amount of the retained austenite and thus the microhardness value declines. Subsequently, by further increasing the annealing time to 7.2 ks, the microhardness value increases again due to decrease in the volume fraction of retained austenite and increase of the amount of precipitates.

sections.heading: Shape memory effect
paragraphs: It is important to note that some key factors are necessary to observe the SME in Fe-based SMAs. The presence of the austenite phase in the macrostructure of the alloy is the first factor. Under straining of the austenite phase, various plastic deformation mechanisms such as sliding of perfect dislocations, mechanical twinning and formation of ε-martensite are possible. For the observation of SME, the transformation of austenite to ε-martensite should be the prominent mechanism of deformation. The mechanism of plastic deformation depends on the stacking-fault energy (SFE). When the SFE in Fe-based SMAs is below 12 mJ/m 2 , austenite to ε-martensite transformation is possible [ 54 , 55 ]. Previous studies showed that the SFE in the present alloy was ∼10 mJ/m 2 , which was below the critical value [ 56 ]. This indicates that the present alloy is susceptible to the transformation of austenite to ε-martensite. Therefore, low SFE is the second factor for observing SME in Fe-based SMAs. The third decisive factor is the need to strengthen the austenite phase in order to prevent the perfect dislocations glide. Therefore, the existence of the austenite phase with a high volume fraction and a high strength in an Fe-based SMA with a relevant SFE less than 12 mJ/m 2  can lead to achieving a high value of SME.

According to  Fig. 10 , the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks exhibits the highest shape recovery for the entire pre-strain range with a maximum value of ∼55% at 1% pre-strain. The maximum recovery strain with a value of ∼1.92% also belongs to this specimen and is achieved at 8% pre-strain ( Fig. 11 ). From  Figs. 5 and 9 , a suitable combination of a relatively high volume fraction of austenite (∼30%) and a high value of microhardness (∼445 Hv) in the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks leads to a maximum value of shape recovery. Although the maximum amount of retained austenite is found in the aged-IA specimen for 3.6 ks (∼45%), the maximum value of shape recovery is not observed in this sample because it has a low value of microhardness (∼360 Hv). On the other hand, although the microhardness is the highest for the aged-IA specimen for 0.9 ks (∼495 Hv), the shape recovery is lower compared to the other samples due to the low percentage of austenite phase (∼17%).

Based on the HRTEM image in  Fig. 12 , the presence of isolated stacking faults in the reversed austenite phase in the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks after applying 1% pre-strain confirms the occurrence of the austenite to ε-martensite transformation (γ→ε) under loading of the material. This suggests that the formation of fine θ-NiMn precipitates in the microstructure of the IA specimen followed by subsequent ageing leads to an increase in the yield strength of the austenite and promotes the martensitic transformation as a prominent deformation mechanism. Also, the observation of SME in the aged-IA specimens in  Fig. 10  proves that strain-induced austenite to ε-martensite transformation (γ→ε) under loading and reverse transformation (ε→γ) on heating are the main causes of shape recovery in the present alloy. It should be noted that the strain-induced γ→ε transformation is induced by the sliding of Shockley partial dislocations. In a specific situation, perfect dislocation change into two Shockley partial dislocations that make a stacking fault between them. The movement of Shockley partial dislocation produces a bulk hcp crystal [ 57 ]. In addition to increasing the yield strength of the austenite phase by precipitation hardening, the precipitates can act as nucleation sites for ε-martensite under straining and promote strain-induced γ→ε transformation [ 21 , 22 , 58 , 59 ]. Moreover, the elastic strain fields surrounding the precipitates exert back stresses on the martensite tips and support the reverse motion of the Shockley partial dislocations at the martensite tips upon heating and thus promote the reverse transformation (ε→γ) [ 21 , 22 , 58 ]. In addition, according to  Fig. 10 (a), the shape recovery for all of the aged-IA specimens continuously decreases by increasing the pre-strain. This decrease is due to the fact that by increasing the pre-strain, the stress exerted on the specimens gradually increases, so that, in addition to the austenite to ε-marteniste phase transformation, other deformation mechanisms such as perfect dislocation slip can be promoted. As a result, the shape recovery decreases by increasing pre-strain. However, it is expected that the shape recovery will gradually merge to a plateau value at higher pre-strains due to structural stability.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
A combination of intercritical annealing in the dual phase (α+γ) region at 590 °C for various annealing times and subsequent ageing at 480 °C for 3.6 ks was applied to an Fe–9Ni-6.5Mn (at.%) steel with an initial lath martensitic microstructure leading to the following results: 
                         
                            1. 
                            EDS, EBSD and HRTEM results revealed that intercritical annealing treatment led to formation of the lath-shaped austenite phase with a diffusionless shear nature in the martensitic matrix so that a dual phase (α′+γ) steel was developed. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Subsequent ageing treatment on the IA specimen caused to nucleation of nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates in the dual phase microstructure. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            A suitable combination of a relatively high volume fraction of austenite (∼30%) and a high value of microhardness (∼445 Hv) in the aged-IA specimen for 1.8 ks led to obtain a maximum value of shape recovery of ∼55%. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The presence of austenite phase reinforced by nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates in the dual-phase steel was the main reason for appearance the shape recovery. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            The existence of isolated stacking faults in the reversed austenite region after straining proved that the occurrence of the austenite to ε-martensite transformation (γ→ε) under loading and its reversion (ε→γ) upon heating are the main causes of the shape memory effect in the developed dual-phase steel.

paragraphs: The raw/processed data required to reproduce these findings cannot be shared at this time as the data form part of an ongoing study.
